Beer and wine are drinks at this stage. Whisky and shochu are made by distilling it.
item.semiconductor-lab.fermented_wash.pl: Approximation: alcohol strength is fixed at about 10%.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note1: The alcohol in drinks. Used to disinfect and to make other chemicals. Burns easily.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note2: 3 fermented wash + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle. Raw material for ethylene [2-36] and chloroform [2-38]; a solvent. ⚠ GHS: flammable, eye irritant.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note3: Ethanol, C2H5OH, boils at 78 C, below water (100 C), so distilling collects it. But at 95.6% the vapour has the same makeup as the liquid (an azeotrope), so distilling cannot make it any stronger.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.note4: To get 100% ethanol you use something that takes only the water (quicklime, molecular sieves), or distil with benzene added.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethanol.placehold: Approximation: making it 100% (anhydrous) is not implemented.
block.semiconductor-lab.alumina_catalyst: Pass alcohol vapour over hot white powder (alumina) and it turns into a gas called ethylene.
6 iron + 3 alumina. Put it on a lit campfire and right-click with ethanol -> 1 bag of ethylene (the bottle is returned). The tube (catalyst) is not used up. A cold tube does not react.
The hot alumina surface pulls water out of ethanol (dehydration): C2H5OH -> C2H4 + H2O. Alumina only helps the reaction and is not used up (a catalyst).
Before oil became cheap, ethylene was made from alcohol this way. Brazil and India still make 'bio-ethylene' from sugarcane alcohol.
Approximation: temperature is only 'over a fire or not'. The water by-product is not collected. The old route of dehydrating with concentrated sulfuric acid is not implemented.
message.semiconductor-lab.alumina_cataly: The tube is cold. Put it on a lit campfire
The ethanol lost water and became ethylene
item.semiconductor-lab.ethylene_gas.note: A sweet-smelling, very flammable gas. The source of polyethylene (plastic bags).
Made from ethanol in an alumina catalyst tube. Becomes polyethylene [2-37] in a high-pressure reactor. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure, specific target organ toxicity (drowsiness).
In ethylene, C2H4, the two carbons share a double bond. When it opens and links to the next ethylene again and again, you get polyethylene.
In 1795 four Dutch chemists called it 'oil-making gas' (with chlorine it makes an oily liquid) ⚠️. Ethylene is also a plant hormone that ripens fruit; it is used to ripen bananas.
item.semiconductor-lab.ethylene_gas.plac: Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The petroleum (naphtha cracking) route is not included (this mod has no crude oil).
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene.note: A light plastic that keeps out water and electricity; used for plastic bags and buckets.
Made from ethylene in a high-pressure reactor. Used for chemical containers and wire insulation. Softens when heated (thermoplastic).
A long chain of tens of thousands of -CH2-CH2- units. Made of only carbon and hydrogen, it resists acids, alkalis, and even hydrofluoric acid.
In World War II it insulated the cables of airborne radar. In chip fabs today, hydrofluoric acid bottles are polyethylene too.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene.plac: Approximation: molecular weight and density are not distinguished.
block.semiconductor-lab.high_pressure_re: A machine that squeezes a gas with huge force and turns it into plastic (polyethylene).
8 steel + compressor. 4 bags of ethylene + oxygen (1 bag lasts 16 runs) -> 1 polyethylene (20 s, 5 kW). Without oxygen it does not start.
Very high pressure (about 1400 atm) packs ethylene molecules close together; a tiny trace of oxygen starts it off (initiator), the double bonds open and link one after another.
In 1933 Fawcett and Gibson at ICI were studying a different reaction and found a white waxy solid in the vessel. Only in 1935 did they learn that oxygen leaking in had started it.
Approximation: pressure and temperature are not given as numbers. Unreacted ethylene is not recycled, and low- vs high-density polyethylene is not distinguished.
A white powder that smells of chlorine. It whitens cloth and disinfects water.
Slaked lime + a bag of chlorine. With ethanol it makes chloroform. ⚠ GHS: oxidizer, skin corrosion, harmful to aquatic life. Mixed with acid it releases chlorine (never mix).
Slaked lime absorbs chlorine and becomes a powder containing calcium hypochlorite. The hypochlorite ion ClO- oxidizes and breaks down dye and germ molecules.
Patented by Tennant in Scotland in 1799. Before that, whitening cloth meant months of laying it in the sun; now it took days.
Approximation: the chamber where lime absorbs chlorine is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note1: A heavy, sweet-smelling liquid. It was once used to put patients to sleep for surgery, but it is harmful, so it is no longer used.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note2: Ethanol + 2 bleaching powder + quartz still (returned) + empty glass bottle (the ethanol bottle is returned too). Raw material for PTFE [2-38] (the next step cannot be made yet); a solvent. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin irritant, carcinogenic (category 2), reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity. Treated only as an industrial material.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note3: Chlorine from the bleaching powder oxidizes ethanol and adds chlorine to it; at the end, the one-carbon CHCl3 is split off (the haloform reaction).
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.note4: In 1831 Guthrie (USA), Soubeiran (France) and Liebig (Germany) each made it independently. Simpson used it as an anaesthetic in 1847. Today it is a raw material for refrigerants and Teflon.
item.semiconductor-lab.chloroform.placeh: Approximation: conditions are not described (DESIGN). By-products (calcium formate, calcium chloride) are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.kelp_ash.placehol: Approximation: real Scottish kelp ash held only a few percent sodium carbonate, mostly potassium salts (here the liquor yields soda). ⚠️
item.semiconductor-lab.polyethylene_bott: A plastic bottle that hydrofluoric acid cannot eat through.
HF dissolves glass, but polyethylene (a chain of -CH2- only) has nothing for it to attack.
Before polyethylene, HF was kept in lead, wax (ceresin) or gutta-percha bottles. Polyethylene was found at ICI in 1933; HF bottles of it came in the 1950s. ⚠️ the exact year is not confirmed.

Polyethylene resists most acids and bases at room temperature, but strong oxidisers (hot concentrated nitric acid) and some solvents soften it. Today very pure HF for chips is shipped in PTFE or high-purity PE.
item.semiconductor-lab.phosphorus_trichl: A sharp-smelling liquid of phosphorus and chlorine. A tool for putting chlorine onto other things.

White phosphorus (the water jar is returned) + 3 bags of chlorine. Used for acetic acid -> acetyl chloride and cinnamic acid -> cinnamoyl chloride. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material.
P4 + 6Cl2 -> 4PCl3. PCl3 swaps the OH of an acid for Cl: 3RCOOH + PCl3 -> 3RCOCl + H3PO3.
First made in 1808 by Gay-Lussac and Thenard. Still made in large amounts for pesticides, flame retardants and medicines.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetyl_chloride.n: Acetic acid with its OH swapped for chlorine. Very reactive.

3 acetic acid + phosphorus trichloride make 3 (no phosphorous acid). + sodium acetate -> acetic anhydride. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material. Flammable.
The Cl next to C=O leaves easily, handing an acetyl group CH3CO- to other molecules.
In 1852 Gerhardt in France made acetic anhydride for the first time, from acetyl chloride and a salt of acetic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.acetyl_chloride.p: Approximation: the phosphorous acid by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_acetate.no: A white salt from neutralizing acetic acid with sodium hydroxide. The filling of reusable hand warmers.
Acetic acid + sodium hydroxide. Material for acetic anhydride and cinnamic acid (the Perkin reaction).
CH3COOH + NaOH -> CH3COONa + H2O. In the Perkin reaction it acts as a weak base that starts things by pulling a hydrogen off acetic anhydride.
Its melted solution can cool without setting (supercooling), then sets all at once when disturbed, giving off heat: that is how reusable hand warmers work.
item.semiconductor-lab.sodium_acetate.pl: Approximation: hydrate water (the trihydrate) is not distinguished.
Two acetic acids with one water taken out. It puts acetyl groups onto other things.

Acetyl chloride + sodium acetate (no salt by-product). Material for cinnamic acid (Perkin reaction) and cellulose acetate (the [2-18] membrane). ⚠ GHS: flammable, acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Treated only as an industrial material.
CH3COCl + CH3COONa -> (CH3CO)2O + NaCl. With water, (CH3CO)2O turns back into two acetic acids.
First made by Gerhardt in 1852. Today it goes into cellulose acetate (cigarette filters, photo film) and aspirin.
Approximation: the modern ketene route is not included. The salt by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note1: Benzene with one CH3 attached. Smells like paint thinner.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note2: 2 light oil + quartz still (returned): finely separating the cut between benzene and xylene (rectification). + 2 chlorine -> benzal chloride. ⚠ GHS: flammable, aspiration hazard, reproductive toxicity, specific target organ toxicity.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note3: Boils at 111 C, between benzene (80 C) and xylene (about 140 C).
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.note4: Named after Tolu balsam from South America; Deville found it in 1841 by distilling that resin.
item.semiconductor-lab.toluene.placehold: Approximation: the number of rectifying stages and purity are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzal_chloride.n: Toluene with two hydrogens of its CH3 swapped for chlorine. One step before benzaldehyde.
Toluene + 2 bags of chlorine. + slaked lime + water bucket -> benzaldehyde. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin and eye irritant, carcinogenic (category 1B). Treated only as an industrial material.
With light or heat, chlorine replaces hydrogens on the CH3 (the side chain), not on the ring: C6H5CH3 + 2Cl2 -> C6H5CHCl2 + 2HCl.
Since the later 19th century this has been a route for making benzaldehyde industrially.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzal_chloride.p: Approximation: light and heat conditions are not modelled. The hydrogen chloride by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzaldehyde.note: A liquid with a sweet almond smell. Raw material for cinnamic acid.
Benzal chloride + slaked lime + water bucket (the empty bucket is returned). + acetic anhydride + sodium acetate -> Perkin mixture. ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (oral).
C6H5CHCl2 + H2O -> C6H5CHO + 2HCl (the lime takes up the hydrogen chloride).
It was taken from bitter almond oil in 1803; in 1832 Liebig and Wohler studied its structure and spread the idea of the 'radical'.
item.semiconductor-lab.benzaldehyde.plac: Approximation: the calcium chloride by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note1: Benzaldehyde mixed with acetic anhydride. Heat it in a furnace to get cinnamic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note2: Benzaldehyde + acetic anhydride + sodium acetate; heat in a furnace for cinnamic acid.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note3: Sodium acetate pulls a hydrogen off acetic anhydride, which then adds to the C=O of benzaldehyde and forms a carbon-carbon double bond: C6H5CHO + (CH3CO)2O -> C6H5CH=CHCOOH + CH3COOH.
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.note4: Perkin found the purple dye mauve at 18 (1856). In 1868 he used this reaction to make coumarin (the scent of fresh hay).
item.semiconductor-lab.perkin_mix.placeh: Approximation: conditions are not described (DESIGN). The acetic acid by-product is not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamic_acid.not: White crystals related to the smell of cinnamon. They stick together when light hits them.
Heat the Perkin reaction mixture in a furnace. 3 + phosphorus trichloride -> 3 cinnamoyl chloride (material for the KPR negative resist).
C6H5CH=CHCOOH. When UV hits the crystal, neighbouring C=C bonds open and join into a four-carbon ring ([2+2] dimerization).
Kodak's 1950s negative photoresist KPR put many of these 'light-sticking' groups onto chains of polyvinyl alcohol.
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamic_acid.pla: Approximation: cis and trans are not distinguished (treated as trans).
item.semiconductor-lab.cinnamoyl_chlorid: Cinnamic acid with its OH swapped for chlorine. A tool for attaching cinnamic acid to other molecules.

3 cinnamic acid + phosphorus trichloride make 3. Attached to polyvinyl alcohol it gives polyvinyl cinnamate (KPR material, not makeable yet). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity, skin corrosion. Reacts violently with water, giving hydrogen chloride. Treated only as an industrial material.
C6H5CH=CHCOCl. The Cl leaves easily and links with the OH of an alcohol to form an ester.
Minsk and colleagues at Kodak made polyvinyl cinnamate from polyvinyl alcohol and cinnamoyl chloride (1950s) ⚠️.
Approximation: the phosphorous acid by-product is not produced.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note1: Seal the lid tight and heat the water inside, and the steam squeezes everything. Heating under that squeeze sets things without bubbles.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note2: 7 steel + copper cable (pressure gauge omitted). 10 kW. Material top-left, water bucket bottom-left (4 runs). As it heats, steam pressure rises (about 5 atm at 150 C, up to 12 atm at the safety valve). Resol mixture -> 2 Bakelite at 150 C and 5 atm or more. Without water or with too little pressure you get foamy Bakelite.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note3: Water heated in a closed vessel stays liquid above its boiling point, and the steam pressure (saturated vapour pressure) climbs steeply with temperature. Same idea as a pressure cooker.
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.note4: Baekeland solved the problem of resol foaming from its own water vapour by holding it down with pressure ('heat and pressure': filed 1907, patented 1909). The vessel was called a 'Bakelizer' ⚠️. ⚠ Accident: a pressure vessel bursts if the safety valve fails or the walls are too thin (the many 19th-century boiler explosions led to safety valves and inspection rules).
block.semiconductor-lab.autoclave.placeh: Approximation: temperature and pressure use a simple model (same form as the Acheson furnace; saturated vapour pressure from the Antoine equation). Mould shapes are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.foamy_bakelite.no: Heated without pressure, so it is full of bubbles and brittle. A failure.
Made by heating resol mixture in a furnace (normal air pressure), or in an autoclave without enough pressure. Not usable for anything else.
As resol sets it gives off water (and a little formaldehyde). Without pressure these turn to gas, make bubbles, and get frozen in.
People before Baekeland had made phenol-formaldehyde resins too, but they came out foamy and brittle and were useless.
item.semiconductor-lab.foamy_bakelite.pl: Approximation: how foamy it is is not modelled (it either works or not).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetylene_gas.not: A very flammable gas that comes off when water hits carbide. The light of old lamps.

Calcium carbide + water bucket (the empty bucket is returned). + acetic acid + mercuric sulfate (catalyst) -> vinyl acetate. ⚠ GHS: flammable gas (category 1), gas under pressure, may decompose explosively even without air.
CaC2 + 2H2O -> C2H2 + Ca(OH)2. Its carbons share a triple bond, so many things can be added onto it.
Willson made carbide by accident in 1892. In the first half of the 20th century, before petroleum, acetylene was a key raw material for plastics and synthetic rubber (acetylene chemistry).
item.semiconductor-lab.acetylene_gas.pla: Approximation: 1 bag = about 1 mol. The slaked lime by-product is not produced.
A white powder that helps things add onto acetylene. A very strong poison.

Mercury (the iron flask is returned) + 2 sulfuric acid. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). ⚠ GHS: acute toxicity (category 1-2), specific target organ toxicity, hazardous to the aquatic environment (long-term). Treated only as an industrial material.
Mercury ions attach to acetylene's triple bond and make it easier to add acetic acid or water.

Lesson: Minamata disease. The Chisso factory in Minamata, Kumamoto, used mercuric sulfate as a catalyst to make acetaldehyde from acetylene and released the methylmercury formed in the reaction into the sea. Many people who ate the fish developed a severe nerve disease (officially recognized in 1956), and some still suffer today. Factories now use methods without mercury.
Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out (the real one is slowly lost). Modern vinyl acetate uses no mercury (zinc or palladium catalysts).
item.semiconductor-lab.vinyl_acetate.not: Acetic acid added onto acetylene. Linked up it becomes polyvinyl acetate (the stuff in wood glue).

Acetylene + acetic acid + mercuric sulfate (catalyst, returned). 4 + hydrogen peroxide (initiator, bottle returned) -> 2 polyvinyl acetate. ⚠ GHS: flammable, specific target organ toxicity, carcinogenic (category 2).
HC≡CH + CH3COOH -> CH2=CHOCOCH3. A C=C double bond remains, so it can be linked into a polymer.
First made by Klatte in Germany in 1912 (Griesheim-Elektron).
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_acetate: A soft resin behind wood glue and chewing gum.
4 vinyl acetate + hydrogen peroxide make 2. + methanol + sodium hydroxide -> polyvinyl alcohol.
Radicals (fragments with an unpaired electron) from hydrogen peroxide open the double bond and link vinyl acetate one after another (radical polymerization).
The white liquid of wood glue is fine particles of polyvinyl acetate spread in water (an emulsion).
Approximation: polymerization temperature and molecular weight are not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_alcohol: A white resin that dissolves in water. In laundry starch and liquid glue.
Polyvinyl acetate + methanol + sodium hydroxide (methyl acetate is not produced). + 2 cinnamoyl chloride -> polyvinyl cinnamate (KPR negative resist material). Also for polarizing film [B-06].
'Vinyl alcohol' itself is unstable and cannot be linked up, so vinyl acetate is linked first and then its acetate parts are swapped for OH (saponification).
Made by Herrmann and Haehnel in Germany in 1924. In Japan the PVA fibre vinylon (Sakurada and others, 1939) went into production in 1950.
Approximation: the degree of saponification is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.polyvinyl_cinnama: A resin that hardens only where light hits it. Material for one of the earliest photoresists used to copy chip patterns.
Polyvinyl alcohol + 2 cinnamoyl chloride. Material for the negative photoresist ([2-30], E's process).

UV makes the C=C of the many cinnamate groups on the chain join with cinnamate on a neighbouring chain into a four-carbon ring ([2+2] dimerization). The chains become bridged, so lit areas no longer dissolve in solvent: a negative resist.

KPR, the photoresist made by Minsk and colleagues at Kodak in the 1950s, was used to pattern the earliest transistors and ICs ⚠️. Later, cyclized rubber + bis-azide resists took over. (Bis-azides explode easily with shock or heat, so this game does not make them and uses the earlier KPR instead.)
Approximation: pyridine (reaction solvent and base) is omitted. Sensitizers that raise the speed are handled in E's process.
item.semiconductor-lab.potassium_dichrom: Bright orange crystals. Very harmful (hexavalent chromium).

2 sodium chromate + sulfuric acid (bottle returns) + potassium carbonate. Heated in a furnace it decomposes to chromium(III) oxide. ⚠ GHS: oxidizing, acute toxicity, skin corrosion, respiratory and skin sensitization, carcinogenicity (category 1B), mutagenicity, reproductive toxicity, aquatic hazard. Handled only as an industrial material.
Adding acid joins two yellow chromate ions into orange dichromate (2CrO4²⁻ + 2H⁺ -> Cr2O7²⁻ + H2O). The potassium salt dissolves poorly, so it crystallizes out easily.

Mixed into gelatin, dichromate hardens where light falls (dichromated gelatin [2-31], an ancestor of photoengraving). A strong oxidizer once used for cleaning lab glassware (chromic acid), now avoided because of its toxicity.
Approximation: really made by double decomposition of sodium dichromate with potassium chloride (potassium carbonate stands in here).
item.semiconductor-lab.antimony_pentachl: A fuming liquid that smells of chlorine. It helps reactions that add fluorine.

Antimony + 3 bags of chlorine. Not used up on the crafting table (catalyst). Used for chloroform + 2 hydrofluoric acid -> R-22. ⚠ GHS: skin corrosion, hazardous to aquatic life. Reacts violently with water. Treated only as an industrial material.
Antimony acts as a 'carrier' that swaps fluorine from hydrogen fluoride for chlorine on the other molecule (the Swarts reaction).
In the 1890s Swarts in Belgium found how to put fluorine on organic compounds with antimony fluorides. The later refrigerant (CFC) industry grew from this.
Approximation: the catalyst does not wear out. Really, part of the SbCl5 turns into fluorides (SbCl3F2 etc.) that do the work.
item.semiconductor-lab.chlorodifluoromet: A gas once used as an air-conditioner refrigerant. Raw material for PTFE.

Chloroform (bottle returned) + 2 hydrofluoric acid (lead bottles returned) + antimony pentachloride (catalyst, returned). In a pyrolysis furnace it becomes TFE. ⚠ GHS: gas under pressure. Damages the ozone layer.
CHCl3 + 2HF -> CHClF2 + 2HCl. Two of chloroform's chlorines are swapped for fluorine.
A member of the CFC family (an HCFC). Because it damages the ozone layer, the Montreal Protocol (1987) led to phasing out its use as a refrigerant; its use as a feedstock continues.
Approximation: the hydrogen chloride by-product is not produced. 1 bag = about 1 mol.
item.semiconductor-lab.tetrafluoroethyle: Ethylene with every hydrogen swapped for fluorine. Linked up, it becomes Teflon (PTFE).

Made from 2 bags of R-22 in a pyrolysis furnace. 4 bags -> PTFE in an autoclave (with water, 80 C or more). ⚠ GHS: flammable gas, gas under pressure, carcinogenic (category 1B). It can polymerize by itself or decompose explosively. Treated only as an industrial material.
2CHClF2 -> C2F4 + 2HCl (about 700 C). When its C=C double bond opens, it links up again and again.
In 1938 Plunkett at DuPont stored TFE in cylinders for refrigerant experiments. Opening the valve gave no gas, yet the cylinder weighed the same. Cut open, it held a slippery white powder: PTFE.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note1: A white plastic that is very slippery, sticks to almost nothing, and dissolves in nothing. The coating of non-stick pans.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note2: Polymerize 4 bags of TFE in an autoclave (with water, 80 C or more). It resists hydrofluoric acid, aqua regia and almost every chemical. Used for chemical pipes and containers in chip fabs.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note3: Long -CF2-CF2- chains. Fluorine wraps the carbon tightly and the C-F bond is very strong, so other molecules cannot get at it.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.note4: Plunkett found it by accident in 1938 when another experiment went wrong. In the Manhattan Project it was used to handle corrosive uranium hexafluoride gas for enriching uranium.
item.semiconductor-lab.ptfe.placeholder: Approximation: real polymerization runs at TFE's own pressure (about 10-30 atm) with a persulfate initiator. This vessel's pressure is only steam, so temperature is the only condition.
block.semiconductor-lab.pyrolysis_furnac: A furnace that sends gas through a platinum tube and heats it until its molecules rearrange.
6 steel + platinum + copper cable. 8 kW. 2 bags of R-22 -> 1 bag of TFE + 2 bags of hydrogen chloride (10 s).

At about 700 C hydrogen chloride leaves chlorodifluoromethane, and two leftover CF2 fragments join into TFE. The tube is platinum, which resists attack even when hot (real ones use platinum, silver or nickel alloys).
Rearranging molecules with heat ('pyrolysis' or 'cracking') is also the heart of making ethylene from petroleum in today's chemical industry.
Approximation: temperature is not given as a number. By-products (such as hexafluoropropylene) are not produced.
item.semiconductor-lab.negative_resist.n: A liquid that hardens and stays where light hits it. Carrying it in sunlight ruins it.

In a glass bottle (the bottle comes back). Crafting: 1 polyvinyl cinnamate (from D) + 1 xylene + 1 empty glass bottle → 1. Coated in the spin coater [9-19] it becomes a negative resist, developed in xylene [9-21]. Holding it in sunlight spoils it. GHS: flammable (solvent).

The cinnamate groups on the polyvinyl cinnamate chains join in pairs under ultraviolet light ([2+2] photodimerisation). Cross-linked chains no longer dissolve; unexposed areas wash away in xylene, hence 'negative'.

Minsk and colleagues at Kodak made it as KPR around 1954; it was the resist when Bell Labs and the US Army applied photoengraving to semiconductors in 1955–57. From 1957 KTFR, based on cyclized rubber, became the main IC resist. Both swell in the developer and cannot print lines much finer than about 2 µm, so positive resist took over in the late 1970s. ⚠️ Real KPR contained a sensitiser so ordinary mercury lamp light exposed it well (no sensitiser here).
item.semiconductor-lab.negative_resist.p: Approximation: no sensitiser (real KPR used one to respond to longer wavelengths). Solvent is xylene.
item.semiconductor-lab.hydrofluoric_acid: The same very dangerous acid, now in a light plastic bottle that will not break.
Pour lead-bottled HF into an empty polyethylene bottle (the lead bottle comes back). Machines take HF in either bottle.
From the 1950s polyethylene bottles replaced lead, wax and gutta-percha for HF: HF dissolves glass but cannot attack the -CH2- chain. ⚠️ the exact year is not confirmed.

HF goes through skin and takes calcium from the body; burns may not hurt at first. Hazard (GHS): fatal on skin contact or if swallowed or inhaled, causes severe burns. Calcium gluconate gel is the first aid.
item.semiconductor-lab.cellulose_acetate: A white powder: wood fibre with acetic acid attached. Used for photo film and cigarette filters.
Wood pulp + 2 acetic anhydride + acetic acid + sulfuric acid (catalyst, bottle returned). 2 + acetone + water bucket -> RO membrane.
Acetic anhydride puts acetyl groups on cellulose's OH groups (esterification). With fewer OH groups it dissolves in solvents like acetone.
First made by Schutzenberger in 1865. It became 'safety film', replacing flammable celluloid movie film.
Approximation: the degree of substitution is not modelled.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note1: A very fine membrane that lets only water through and holds back dissolved salts.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note2: 2 cellulose acetate + acetone (dissolve and spread) + water bucket (set it). A part of the ultrapure water system.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note3: Normally water moves by itself toward the stronger solution (osmosis). Push the strong side harder than the osmotic pressure and only water is squeezed back the other way (reverse osmosis).
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.note4: Around 1960 Loeb and Sourirajan at UCLA made an 'asymmetric' membrane, very dense only at the surface and porous below, which passed water fast enough to make fresh water from seawater.
item.semiconductor-lab.ro_membrane.place: Approximation: the partial drying time and additive (magnesium perchlorate) in casting are omitted.
item.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water.n: The cleanest water, with almost no ions or germs. Used to wash chips.
Made from deionized water in the ultrapure water system (filled into a polyethylene bottle). Resistivity 18.2 MOhm·cm (25 C). Used for wafer cleaning and rinsing ([9-14]).

Water molecules themselves split very slightly into H+ and OH- (10^-7 mol/L each). Only that conducts, so resistivity cannot go above 18.2 MOhm·cm. In a glass bottle, sodium and other ions would leach out of the glass.
Ion-exchanged pure water was used in chip plants from the 1950s, and the term 'ultrapure water' spread from the late 1970s-80s ⚠️. Today a fab uses thousands of tonnes a day.
item.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water.p: Approximation: resistivity is fixed at 18.2 MOhm·cm (its drop over time as CO2 from the air dissolves is not modelled).
block.semiconductor-lab.ultrapure_water_: A three-stage system (ion exchange, filtering, UV) that removes almost every impurity from water.

4 polyethylene + mercury lamp tube (UV) + 2 ion exchange columns + RO membrane + copper cable. 1 kW. Deionized water (glass bottle) + empty polyethylene bottle -> ultrapure water + empty glass bottle (5 s). Plain distilled water is not accepted (run it through an ion exchange column first).
Water goes through distillation -> ion exchange (ions) -> reverse osmosis (organics, particles, germs) -> UV at 254 nm (kills germs, breaks down organics).
Real systems keep water circulating nonstop: if it stands still, germs grow in the pipes and CO2 from the air dissolves, lowering the purity.
Approximation: membrane fouling, recirculation and resistivity measurement are not modelled.
